## Simplices and complexes

These building blocks have a common name. A vertex is a **0-simplex**, an edge
is a **1-simplex**, and a filled triangle is a **2-simplex**. More generally,
an abstract $p$-simplex is a set of $p+1$ vertices,

$$
\sigma=[v_0,\ldots,v_p].
$$

Its dimension is $\dim\sigma=p$. A **face** is any simplex obtained from a
subset of these vertices. A **codimension-one face** removes exactly one
vertex.

::: {.column-margin .study-note .insight}
**Why “codimension”?** The codimension of a face inside a simplex is the
difference between their dimensions. Removing one vertex lowers the dimension
by one, so the resulting face has codimension one.
:::

A **finite abstract simplicial complex** on a vertex set $V$ is a collection
$K$ of non-empty finite subsets of $V$ such that

$$
\sigma\in K,\quad \varnothing\ne\tau\subseteq\sigma
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tau\in K.
$$

::: {.column-margin .study-note .qualification}
**What is required of $K$?** For the abstract complexes used here, downward
closure is the defining compatibility condition. Finiteness is a separate
assumption that keeps the course calculations and software finite. A
geometrically embedded simplicial complex must also satisfy geometric
intersection conditions, but its abstract incidence structure is still
downward closed.
:::

The dimension of $K$ is the largest dimension of any simplex in $K$. The
condition above is **downward closure**: whenever a simplex belongs to $K$,
all of its faces must belong to $K$ as well. A filled triangle therefore
brings its three edges and three vertices with it.

::: {.column-margin .study-note .insight}
**Why downward closure?** Homology will take the boundary of each simplex. Its
faces must already be simplices of $K$, otherwise the boundary map would leave
the vector spaces built from $K$. Filtrations later require every stage to be
a valid complex, but tracking birth and death is not the reason for imposing
this rule.
:::

For example,

$$
\{[v_0],[v_1],[v_2],[v_0,v_1],[v_1,v_2],[v_0,v_2],[v_0,v_1,v_2]\}
$$

is a simplicial complex. The collection

$$
\{[v_0],[v_1],[v_2],[v_0,v_1,v_2]\}
$$

is not, because it contains a triangle while omitting its edges.

::: {.column-margin .study-note .audience-dynamics}
**Graph, hypergraph or simplicial complex?** A graph records pairwise
relations. A hypergraph may record a five-person interaction without asserting
that every pair interacted. A simplicial complex includes every lower-order
face, so turning that hyperedge into a simplex adds all subgroup relations.
That is a modelling decision, not merely a change of notation.
:::

<span id="subcomplexes-inclusions-and-skeletons"></span>

A **subcomplex** $L\subseteq K$ is a collection of simplices from $K$ that is
itself downward closed. The **inclusion**

$$
\iota:L\hookrightarrow K
$$

sends each simplex of $L$ to that same simplex in $K$.

::: {.column-margin .study-note .insight}
**Reading $L\hookrightarrow K$.** The hooked arrow signals inclusion. Here
$K$ is larger only as a collection of simplices: it contains everything in
$L$, and possibly more. A subcomplex really is a subset, but a special one;
an arbitrary subset of the simplices of $K$ may fail downward closure.
:::

The **$p$-skeleton** $K^{(p)}$ contains every simplex of dimension at most
$p$. In particular, $K^{(1)}$ is the graph formed by the vertices and edges.
It omits filled triangles and every higher-dimensional simplex.

<span id="clique-complexes"></span>

For a graph $G$, the **clique complex** $\mathrm{Cl}(G)$, also called its flag
complex, contains one simplex for every complete subgraph. Three mutually
adjacent vertices produce a 2-simplex; four produce a 3-simplex together with
all of its faces. Thus a graph and its clique complex have the same vertices
and edges but need not have the same first homology.

::: {.column-margin .study-note .insight}
**Flag or clique?** The terms are interchangeable. *Flag complex* is common
in topology and algebra, while *clique complex* is common in combinatorics and
network science.
:::

<span id="geometric-realisation-and-triangulation"></span>

Assigning locations to vertices and drawing their convex hulls gives a
**geometric realisation**. The abstract incidence information, not the
coordinates of one drawing, defines the complex. The notation $|K|$ denotes
the space obtained by gluing geometric simplices according to those
incidences. When $|K|$ represents a continuous space, $K$ is a
**triangulation** of that space.

<details class="reader-example">
<summary><span class="reader-example-label">Example</span><span class="reader-example-title">The house complex</span></summary>
<div class="reader-example-body" markdown="1">

The labelled house combines two edge cycles with one filled triangular face.

![The labelled house simplicial complex.](../../assets/topic02-house-complex.svg){fig-alt="Five labelled vertices form a house. Six labelled edges form the outside and the roof-base, and the triangular roof is filled as a two-simplex."}

Its vertices are $v_0,\ldots,v_4$. Its six edges are

$$
x=[v_0,v_1],\quad y=[v_1,v_2],\quad z=[v_2,v_3],
$$

$$
u=[v_3,v_4],\quad v=[v_4,v_0],\quad w=[v_4,v_1],
$$

and its only 2-simplex is the filled roof
$t=[v_0,v_1,v_4]$. Downward closure supplies the edges and vertices of $t$.

The 1-skeleton contains two visible edge cycles, the roof and the room. The
full complex also contains $t$, so the roof cycle is filled while the room
cycle is not. This distinction is what the homology calculation must detect.

</div>
</details>

You are ready to continue when you can read the formal downward-closure rule,
form a subcomplex, identify a skeleton and explain what clique filling adds to
a graph.
